newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mulls evacuating Kurd aid workers from Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mulls evacuating Kurd aid workers from Iraq.

text.p: The United States said on Monday it was still considering whether to evacuate several thousand local aid workers from northern Iraq but did not believe they were in imminent danger.

After a Baghdad-backed Kurdish faction seized control of the area, Washington last month evacuated some 2,100 relief workers directly employed by the U.S. government. Last weekend it took out a further 600 Iraqi opposition activists.
The group still left in northern Iraq, which had been protected from Iraqi forces by Western warplanes since 1991, consists of employees of Western non-governmental organisations, many of them Kurds.

"We are trying to compile as much information on who these people are and what their numbers are as we can. And at some point we'll make a decision," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns. "But we have not yet made the decision to bring them out."

"We'll continue to look at it. Should we feel obviously that the lives of these people are in imminent danger, that would be a compelling factor in any decision that we made. That is not currently the case," he added.
Some U.S. organisations argue that, contrary to the assurances of the U.S. government, the aid workers still in northern Iraq are in danger.
Burns told a news briefing the issue had received "very high-level attention" in the last few days.
Assistant Secretary of State Robert Pelletreau, who is currently visiting the region, had also raised it with leaders of both Kurdish factions battling in northern Iraq, he said.
Both groups "have said that they will, in essence, act to help these people, to make sure that there's no political retribution taken against these people," Burns said.

The 600 people evacuated into Turkey at the weekend will be flown to the U.S. Pacific territory of Guam, where the 2,100 previously evacuated have already been taken, to be processed for asylum in the United States, Burns said.

Burns would not directly confirm that the new group consists largely of members of the Iraqi National Congress, an umbrella group for Iraqi opposition movements. But in response to questions he hinted that this was so.

Burns said although the asylum-screening process in Guam would take several months, he believed the "overwhelming majority" of the applicants would be successful. He declined to predict what would happen to anyone who was refused asylum.
